column2: Especially is it reckoned there for the gift of shraddha, O Bharata; by the gift of food, O king, the excellent fruit is declared.
All this I have told you because of your devotion, O Bharata.
No kinsman equal to a son is seen on earth, who protects one falling into the dreadful sword-leaf forest.
In famines, in distress and in old age too there is the son; without a son, good lady, what use is life even with wealth?
Even when a son is overcome by diseases or weary of the world, fearing people's shame, he is fit to perform the purifying rites.
Endowed with these virtues, a son is good whether he has qualities or not; for one without a son, where is happiness in this world or the next?
Brooding on it by day and at midnight, always, my limbs dry up like shallow streams in summer.
Anasuya said: "All that you have indicated, brahmin, I grieve over; what distresses you burns in my heart.
Sons who will be long-lived and endowed with virtues — I am considering the deed by which Prajapati will be pleased."
Atri said: "I have practised austerity hard to perform since birth, good lady, with vows, fasts, restraints and a diet of vegetables, lovely one.
I see my body wasted and I am unable, fair-faced one; I grieve for myself as I remain — I have told you my secret."
Anasuya said: "Husband, a devoted wife increases her husband and sons; she accomplishes the three aims and is to be served among many people.
Japa, austerity, pilgrimage, and the accomplishment of mantras and worship for a son — all the gurus declare this, as the guru's word has stated.
If you permit me in this sorrow, I shall practise hard austerity; desiring a son, I shall go for many days to the best of gods."
Atri said: "Well done, well done, wise one who gives me contentment; permitted by me, good lady, practise austerity for a son.
Free us from our debt to the gods, men and ancestors; there is no kinsman equal to a wife in the three worlds.
The gods do not praise happiness without a wife; she turns toward one who turns toward her and turns away from one who turns away;
therefore gods, asuras and men praise the wife. At an auspicious moment, you of great vows, great wisdom and true form,
practise austerity quickly for a son, by my command." At the end of these words she prostrated with eight limbs and said:
By your grace, chief of brahmins, may I obtain all this. Going with the playful gait of a swan, the lovely-eyed fair lady,
Anasuya, in her difficult state, reached the river Narmada — equal to Somanatha; there is no need for deliberation.
Those who remember it by day or by night even from hundreds of yojanas away are freed from all sins and dwell in Rudra's world.
Near the Narmada, on both banks and within two yojanas, the fair lady entered upon austerity there at the Reva,
by the mere sight of whom the accumulation of sin perishes. Then on its northern bank the lovely one lived on leaves,
the wide-eyed beauty keeping observances on a diet of vegetables, restrained, praising the gods with auspicious hymns.
In summer the great lady practised the five fires; in the rainy season, in wet clothes, she kept the chandrayana vow;
when winter came she dwelt in the water; at dawn she bathed, then did the twilight rite and made offerings to the gods and others,
worshipping the gods and performing oblation according to rule. When a hundred years had thus passed, Vishnu, Rudra and the Grandsire
came in the form of brahmins to the confluence of the Erandi; standing before her, they recited the Veda.
Anasuya stopped her japa, looked at them again and again, rose, the wide-eyed one, and gave them guest-water according to rule:
Today my birth is fruitful, today my austerity is fruitful; by the sight of brahmins one is freed from all sins.
Then, circumambulating them, she prostrated with eight limbs and said: "Today I shall satisfy you with divine bulbs, roots and fruits."
The brahmins said: "By your wondrous austerity and your truth, lady of good vows, we are satisfied with all desires by the sight of an ascetic woman.
Curiosity has arisen in us: why do you practise austerity? You practise hard austerity to secure heaven or liberation?"
Anasuya said: "By austerity heaven is won, by austerity the supreme goal; by austerity, brahmins, one obtains every desire."
The brahmins said: "Slender, youthful, wide-eyed, of smooth limbs and endowed with beauty, with the playful gait of a swan — why do you dry yourself up?"
Anasuya said: "Austerity should be done in youth; in youth is the supreme goal; in youth the birth of sons; in old age everything is unpleasant."
The brahmins said: "Well done, well done, wise one; ask a boon, lady of good vows; whatever you desire we shall give you in full.
I am Vishnu, I am Rudra, I am the Grandsire himself — bearing hidden forms in the world, marked by our own signs."
At the end of her words they showed their true forms; the gods stood in their own forms, shining like crores of suns:
four-armed Vasudeva bearing conch, discus and mace, Janardana of the colour of the flax flower, clad in yellow,
Hari whose mount is Garutmat, together with Shri, of gracious face and glorious, stood in auspicious form;
clad in white, the fortunate one with four faces, mounted on a swan, holding a rosary in his hand, sinless,
Brahma, Grandsire of the world, had come to the bank of the Narmada; mounted on the bull, with ten arms,
his limbs smeared with ash, five-faced and three-eyed, with a crown of matted hair and the half-moon as his crest —
bearing this form was the god Maheshvara, the all-pervading. And Anasuya there, at the supreme sight of the gods,
trembling in that secluded place, looked at them again and again: "I am declared Brahma, I Vishnu, I Rudra."
Seeing them, the lady of great vows was filled with joy. Anasuya said: "What are your functions, and who are you — Vishnu, Rudra and the Grandsire?
I wish to hear it; tell me this question." Brahma said: "I am called the rainy season and am proclaimed as the waters;
I am called the form of the clouds; I rain upon the earth. I am all beings, the morning twilight when the sun has risen.
For this reason the secret of my nature has been told by me." Vishnu said: "Because of being the winter, the moving and unmoving is of Vishnu's form;
the whole world is to be protected — that is Vishnu's excellent greatness." Rudra said: "I am called the hot season, destroyer of all beings;
in Rudra's form I dry up the whole world, ascetic lady." Thus Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra, lord of the earth —
three twilights, three gods, three times, three fires — so Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra came to oneness.
We give you a boon, good lady, whatever is in your mind. Anasuya said: "I am always proclaimed barren by the people in the world.
Since Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra are gracious and well disposed, the three gods, though unassailable, are well pleased with me;
let them now grant me the boon of their presence at this holy place." The gods said: "Let your words be as you have asked, auspicious one;
Vishnu's maya is manifest here, named Erandi." Anasuya said: "If the three gods are pleased, awakened by my devotion,
let Hari, Rudra and the Grandsire become my sons here." Vishnu said: "I have never heard of givers of wealth becoming sons.
Good lady, I will give you sons equal in valour to the gods, endowed with virtues like their father's, soma-sacrificers, deeply learned."
Anasuya said: "What I have asked, Hari, should be given; it must not be done otherwise — let them dwell in my womb."
The Blessed Lord said: "Long ago, in the dialogue with Bhrigu, dwelling in the womb was incurred by me, and I see no end of it, lovely one.
Remembering what happened long ago, I reflect again and again." As the Grandsire and Maheshvara reflected thus:
We shall be your sons not born of a womb, lovely one; the gods do not dwell in a womb, fair-faced one.
Having said this, they were manifest together with her then; the three gods went to the northern bank of the Narmada, son of Pritha.
The lady obtained her dear boon on the Mahendra mountain; that woman, her body wasted, dried up and most gaunt,
wearing the sacred thread, devoted to austerity, fair-eyed, seated on a flat rock, saw her husband of great vows.
Delighted and content, the great lady said, "Stay, husband." Seeing her, the wise sage spoke to his wife again.
Atri said: "Well done, well done, wise Anasuya of great vows; you have obtained a rare boon impossible for all women."
Anasuya said: "By your grace, great sage, I have obtained a rare boon; by it I give you sons, sages rich in austerity."
Having said this, the lady, filled with great joy, then looked at her husband, and he too at the fair-eyed one.
From that very look an auspicious disc arose on his forehead, surrounded by a net of rays nine thousand yojanas wide,
shaped like a kadamba ball, a threefold circle; in its midst was the lord of gods, a person bearing a divine form,
that god of golden colour, shining like crores of suns, the first son of Anasuya, the Grandsire himself,
the son renowned as Chandramas, Soma, prince, the beloved and excellent son, endowed with sixteen digits:
the first, second and third, O king, the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh and eighth,
the ninth, tenth and the further eleventh, the twelfth, thirteenth and then the fourteenth,
then the fifteenth, the goddess proclaimed as the full moon; the new moon is renowned as the sixteenth digit.
Becoming subtle, fair-faced one, for the fourfold world, this Soma nourishes the whole world with the moving and unmoving.
Gods and asuras, gandharvas, rakshasas and serpents, pishachas, Adityas, the ancestors and the Grandsire —
all live on him; the offered substance abides in him. When Soma has entered the plants, whoever cuts a plant
suffers sorrow, the fool, and burns up a year's good deeds; when Soma has entered the plants, whoever chews a tooth-stick
has eaten the moon and destroyed the line of his ancestors. On the new moon, king of kings, one should bathe according to rule;
for a year, wide-eyed one, the ancestors have the supreme goal. Whoever gives gold, silver and clothing to the twice-born
obtains everything a lakh-fold, O king, no doubt. Distinguished by these qualities is that Prajapati in the form of Soma,
born as the first son, the delight of Anasuya. The second, fortunate one, was named Durvasas,
the maker of creation and dissolution, Maheshvara himself; even Indra was cursed by that second son, fair-faced one.
The birth of the second son has been told by me. The third, by name Dattatreya, is Madhusudana,
the all-pervading lord of the world, the god Janardana himself, who descended, fortunate one, together with Brahma and Shambhu.
The holy place Putraptipada on the northern bank of the Narmada, made by Anasuya, son of Pritha, destroys all sins.
Bathing in the Reva near the confluence is rare, set apart by a hand's breadth in the holy field, lord of men.
Bathing at Suvarnashilaka one attains supreme, auspicious peace. Having fashioned the god Bhaskara, one should offer into the fire
with bilva fruit mixed with ghee and with abundant bilva leaves: "May the lord of the world be pleased; may my disease always perish."
If it is offered to brahmins, one obtains the fruit of a sacrifice; delighted in mind by giving there, one attains heaven at death.
On the eighth of the bright fortnight, fasting and with senses controlled, whatever man performs shraddha there with devotion to men and gods
raises ten generations before and ten after in his family. Whoever gives gold or a very fine cow
goes to the supreme place where the god Maheshvara is. By worshipping Shiva there, one gains victory over enemies,
has sons and virtues and is free of all diseases. Thus, O king, I have told of the excellent Sauvarna holy place.
Markandeya said: In this stretch is the excellent holy place Karandeshvara, famous in all worlds, on the northern bank of the Narmada,
declared to remove all sins and excellent in destroying all sorrows. Then, king of kings, one should go to a supremely lovely holy place,
divine, granting good fortune and destroying men's sin. There, prince, an unlucky woman or man
who bathes and worships Uma and Rudra obtains good fortune. On the third day, fasting for a day and a night with senses controlled,
one should invite a handsome brahmin with his wife there, adorn them with sandal and garlands and perfume them with flowers and incense,
and feed them with devotion with milk-rice or krishara; having fed them duly, one should circumambulate them:
You are the god Mahadeva with your consort, bull-bannered one; as there is never separation for you, god, lord of gods...
Meditating on him here out of humility toward the one called Somanatha — on the bright third of Jyeshtha, in the Saubhagya water of the Narmada,
having bathed and given, a fortunate woman is not separated from her beloved. Yudhishthira said: "No misfortune, no poverty, no grief and no bad goal —
tell me all by which all this may come about." Markandeya said: Misfortune, a bad goal, poverty that increases grief,
and widowhood do not arise for seven births, Yudhishthira; I shall tell you the deed by which sins are destroyed.
In the month of Jyeshtha, in the bright fortnight, especially on the third, whoever bathes there with devotion and practises the austerity of the five fires
is freed from all sins, no doubt. Whoever burns guggulu near Gauri and Shiva —
in that rite what is stated for a brahmin comes about; when the body falls, heaven — so said Shankara.
With various fine garments, white, red and yellow, having honoured brahmin women and brahmin men according to rule,
with many kinds of flowers and splendid perfumes and incense, placing a thread on the neck, one should anoint them with saffron;
regarding the woman as Gauri and the brahmin as Shiva, one should give to them respectfully, releasing the gift with water:
earrings, an armlet and a gold ring; the seven grains and food should also be given, best of kings,
and other gifts at that holy place, best of men; whatever merit there is from all gifts, that merit becomes threefold,
even a thousandfold there; there is no need for deliberation. One enjoys unsurpassed pleasures there together with Shankara;
one's good fortune becomes abundant, no doubt; the sonless obtains a son and the poor man gains wealth.
The wish-granting king of holy places is situated on the Narmada.
Austerity was practised by the giver of wealth, and the lotus-born one was pleased; there, by giving his own property, he obtained endless wealth.
Whoever goes there with devotion, bathes and gives wealth, for him there is never any curtailment of wealth.
Right after it, O king, is the excellent Rohinitirtha, famed in the three worlds, supremely removing all sins.
Yudhishthira said: "I wish to hear from you the greatness of Rohinitirtha, which destroys all sins; you should tell it to me."
Markandeya said: In that dreadful single ocean, when the moving and unmoving had perished, as the god of gods lay upon it, son of Pandu,
a great lotus arose from his navel, like the disc of the sun, furnished with pericarp and filaments and adorned with petals.
There Brahma arose, with four lotus faces; pondering in himself, "What shall I do, lord of gods?"
the blessed Marichi came into being there, lord of the Bharatas; from Marichi was born Kashyapa, maker of all creation.
Then fifty daughters were born to Daksha too; he gave ten to Dharma and thirteen to Kashyapa,
and likewise twenty-seven other daughters to the Moon; among them the one named Rohini, with a face like the lord of stars,
was dearest of all the women, and especially to her husband. Again, resolved upon austerity, lord of men,
she then practised vast austerity on the bank of the Narmada, with fasts of one night, two nights, six, twelve and others,
and fasts of a fortnight and a month, wasting her body, ever worshipping the slayer of the asura Mahisha,
bathing again and again daily in the water of the Narmada, pure and smiling. Then the fortunate goddess Narayani was pleased, O king:
I am pleased with you, fortunate one, by your vows and observances; I will give it you without doubt — choose a boon as you wish.
Hearing these words, Rohini, beloved of the Moon, chose a boon and spoke these words to the goddess:
That I may soon become dearest to the Moon above all my co-wives — make it so by your grace.
So be it, she was told by Bhavani, and praised by hosts of devoted gods, the goddess vanished right there.
From that time the lady Rohini, beloved of the Moon, became dear to all the world, best of kings.
Whatever woman or man bathes with devotion at that holy place becomes dear to their spouse as Rohini is.
Whoever gives up his life at those holy places has no separation for seven births.
Markandeya said: Then, king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Chakratirtha, renowned as Senapura, destroying all sins.
Mahasena was consecrated there as general by the discus-bearing god of gods, together with the gods headed by the king of the gods,
for the slaying of the danava and the victory of the dwellers in heaven, having duly satisfied the chief brahmins with gifts of land,
with the sound of conches and kettledrums and the noise of drums, with vinas, mridangas, jhallaris and bronze cymbals.
Hearing that dreadful sound, a danava proud of his strength, to thwart the gods, came before the consecration,
full of elephants, horses, chariots and foot soldiers, clamorous.
Then, having destroyed that fierce army with very sharp arrows loosed from the fine Sharnga bow, the great-souled slayer of Madhu shattered the elephants, horses and chariots and released his discus.
Seeing the dreadful discus spreading everywhere, the six-faced one left his post there and practised vast austerity.
The discus, released for destruction by Hari, upholder of the worlds, burned the distraught one and fell into the clear water;
it became sinless by the power of the Narmada. In the rainy season, in the bright fortnight, on the twelfth, O Bharata,
whoever, having conquered anger, goes to Chakratirtha, dear to Hari, is freed from sins and does not see dreadful Yama.
Keeping vigil at night, one should have a lamp offered to the god, and a Vaishnava story there, collected on the god of gods.
The Bhima vow, the paraka, the krichchhra and the chandrayana, the santapana vow and the three-night vow intensely —
at the end one crosses the Vaitarani and the dreadful wheel day and night, and never sees the kutashalmali trees.
All this I have told you, the fruit of Chakratirtha.
With pearls the size of the moon's disc, with coral branches and with sapphires,
Varuna, lord of rivers, then gave her guest-offering; all the rivers headed by the Ganga, the Tapi and the Payoshni,
the Nandini and the holy Nalini all gave guest-offering then. Narmada said: "Those who bathe at my divine confluence and make offerings,
I rescue those born in their seven families, no doubt." Then, having offered a handful of water, the Ocean spoke:
I am blessed, I have achieved my purpose, since you have come, fair-faced goddess; blessings on you — purify me here.
Narmada said: "You alone are pure, fortunate great ocean." Markandeya said: Thus, O king, the blessed, auspicious Narmada Mekala
was honoured even by the Ocean, seated on an auspicious throne; she was taken in marriage by Purukutsa, O Bharata.
She, the wife of Purukutsa, joined with the duty of the household, always dwells right there at the auspicious confluence, O king.
Then there was a rain of flowers at the great festival of the gods; there the river held her self-choice, lord of the earth.
Whoever performs shraddha there and offerings to the ancestors obtains the fruit of a lakh of sacrifices and is freed, no doubt.
Thus the Narmada, purifier of the world, worshipped by the three worlds — her incomparable greatness has been proclaimed to you, mighty-armed one.
Hearing it with devotion, fortunate one, one is honoured in Rudra's world. The excellent greatness of the Reva, at its beginning, middle and end —
whoever hears it with devotion obtains the fruit he desires. The man with senses controlled who hears this incomparable greatness
and then gives gifts attains the fulfilment of all desires and aims. Having worshipped the book with incense, lamp and sandal,
one should give gifts there and honour brahmins too; by hearing and giving, the Narmada becomes well pleased.
It has been told before, at each holy place, delight of Pandu; having heard the holy greatness, it is by giving, son of Pandu —
for this reason, having heard, giving is the cause. Hearing these words spoken by Markandeya, the tiger among kings
offered guest-water duly and always honoured the sages; with horses, elephants and chariots, the king of dharma with his brothers,
Yudhishthira quickly made a pilgrimage on the Narmada, bathing, drinking and immersing himself on the northern and southern banks.
The elephants' tusks, hard as the tip of the thunderbolt, have shattered; this is not my strength. This is the power of remembering Janardana, which destroys great calamities and sins.
Kindle a fire, asuras; withdraw, elephants of the quarters. Wind, fan the fire; let this doer of evil be burned.
Then the danavas, urged on by their master, kindled a fire and burned the son of the lord of the asuras, buried under a great heap of wood.

Father, though fanned by the wind this fire does not burn me; all around me I see all the quarters cool, as if strewn with beds of lotuses. This whole triple world with its moving and unmoving — Vishnu, the victorious, the mighty, the praiseworthy, who adorns it and does not bear with evil — him, the steadfast, I praise always, always, forever.
Then the brahmin priests, sons of Bhargava, great-souled and eloquent, praising the lord of the daityas with conciliation, said to him:
O king, restrain your anger toward this child, your own son; your anger toward the hosts of the gods is where it bears fruit. Then Hiranyakashipu, addressed thus by his own priests —

We shall so instruct this child of yours, O king, that he will become disciplined for the destruction of your enemies.
vishnupurana:17:51	Childhood is the seat of all faults, king of the daityas; therefore you should not direct excessive anger at this child.
vishnupurana:17:52	If at our word he does not abandon Hari's side, then we shall produce a kritya that cannot be turned back, to slay him.
Thus entreated by those priests, the king of the daityas had his son taken out of the pile of fire by the daityas.
Then, dwelling in his guru's house, the boy taught the young danavas again and again in the intervals of his guru's instruction:

Hear the highest truth from me, sons of Diti; do not think otherwise of it, for there is no motive of greed or the like in it.
vishnupurana:17:56	Every creature attains birth, then childhood and then youth; then day by day old age comes on, unhindered,
vishnupurana:17:57	and then the creature goes to death, sons of the lord of the daityas; this is seen plainly by us and by you.
vishnupurana:17:58	And for one who has died there is birth again; this is not otherwise. This is the teaching of scripture, and there is no arising without a cause.
vishnupurana:17:59	From dwelling in the womb onward, as long as rebirth goes on, understand every state to be nothing but sorrow.
vishnupurana:17:60	The calming of hunger and thirst, and likewise the relief of cold and the like, one thinks to be happiness through childish understanding; but it is sorrow again.
vishnupurana:17:61	For those whose limbs are utterly stiff, who seek ease in exercise, for men of deluded understanding, even a blow seems pleasure.
vishnupurana:17:62	Where is the body, a great heap of phlegm and all the rest, and where are qualities such as bodily beauty, fragrance and loveliness?
vishnupurana:17:63	If the fool takes delight in a body that is a mass of flesh, blood, pus, excrement, urine, sinew, marrow and bone, he will delight in hell too.
vishnupurana:17:64	Fire is made pleasant by cold, water by thirst, food by hunger; and their opposites are made pleasant by the others.
vishnupurana:17:65	As much as a man takes possession of, sons of the daityas, just so much sorrow it gives to his mind.
vishnupurana:17:66	As many attachments dear to the mind as a creature forms, so many darts of grief are driven into his heart.
vishnupurana:17:67	Whatever is in the house stays in his mind wherever he may be; the thought of its loss, burning or theft remains right there.
vishnupurana:17:68	There is great sorrow at birth here and for one who is dying, fierce torment in Yama's tortures and in passing into the womb.
vishnupurana:17:69	If you infer even a trace of happiness in the womb, then say so; thus the whole world is full of sorrow.
vishnupurana:17:70	So in this ocean of existence, the abode of extreme sorrows, I tell you the truth: Vishnu alone is the refuge.
vishnupurana:17:71	Do not think, 'We are children'; the embodied one is eternal in bodies. Old age, youth, birth and the rest are properties of the body, not of the self.
vishnupurana:17:72	'I am a child now; when I am young I shall strive for my good as I wish; I am young; when old age comes I shall do what is good for myself.
vishnupurana:17:73	I am old; all my duties are beyond my reach; what shall I, feeble, do, when I did nothing while I was able?'
vishnupurana:17:74	Thus a man whose mind is always distracted by false hope never, though thirsting, turns toward his good.
vishnupurana:17:75	In childhood they are attached to toys, in youth they turn to sense objects, and through ignorance and weakness old age arrives.
vishnupurana:17:76	Therefore one of discerning mind should always strive for his good in childhood, unattached to the bodily states of childhood, youth, old age and the rest.
vishnupurana:17:77	This I have told you; if you know it is not false, then to please me remember Vishnu, the giver of release from bondage.
vishnupurana:17:78	What toil is there in remembering him? Remembered, he bestows what is good, and sin is destroyed for those who remember him day and night.
vishnupurana:17:79	Let your minds turn in friendship day and night to him who abides in all beings; thus you will cast off all afflictions.
vishnupurana:17:80	Since this whole world is struck by the three kinds of suffering, what wise man would feel hatred toward beings who are to be pitied?
vishnupurana:17:81	If beings are fortunate while I am weaker, still one should rejoice, for the fruit of hatred is loss.
vishnupurana:17:82	If beings bound by enmity show hatred, then, alas, they are to be pitied by the wise as pervaded by great delusion.
vishnupurana:17:83	These, daityas, are the alternatives of those whose vision is divided, as I have told them; accepting them for argument's sake, hear my summary.
vishnupurana:17:84	This whole universe is the expansion of Vishnu, who is all beings; therefore the discerning should regard it as their own self, without difference.
vishnupurana:17:85	Therefore give up the asura nature; let you and we alike so strive that we may attain bliss —
vishnupurana:17:86	that which is not destroyed by fire, sun, moon or wind, by Parjanya or Varuna, by siddhas or rakshasas,
vishnupurana:17:87	by yakshas or lords of the daityas, by serpents or kinnaras, by men or beasts, or by faults arising in oneself,
vishnupurana:17:88	by fever, eye disease, dysentery, spleen, tumour and the like, or by hatred, jealousy, envy, passion, greed and the rest —
vishnupurana:17:89	which is not brought to an end by anything else, eternal and utterly pure: that a man attains by fixing his heart on the stainless Keshava.
vishnupurana:17:90	I tell you emphatically: find no delight in the turnings of this worthless worldly existence. Daityas, attain equanimity everywhere; equanimity is the worship of Achyuta.
vishnupurana:17:91	When he is pleased, what is there here that cannot be gained? Enough of dharma, wealth and desire — they are paltry. Taking refuge in the endless tree of Brahman, you will without doubt obtain the great fruit.

Those who came to kill me, those who gave poison, those who lit the fire, the elephants of the quarters by whom I was trampled and the serpents by whom I was bitten —
vishnupurana:18:40	toward them and toward my friends I am equal and never sinful; by that truth let the priests of the asuras live today.
When he had spoken thus and touched them, all those brahmins rose up free of disease and spoke to the modest boy:
Be long-lived and unobstructed, endowed with strength and valour, blessed with sons, grandsons, wealth and power — be the best, child.
Having said this to him, the priests then went and told the king of the daityas everything as it had happened, great sage.
Thus the wise, knowing Hari to consist of all beings, should practise unswerving devotion toward all beings.
Hearing this, the lord of the daityas, standing on the top of his palace, his face darkened with rage, said to the daitya servants:
Throw the wicked one down from this palace a hundred yojanas high; let him fall on the mountainside, his limbs shattered on the rocks.
Then all the daitya servants threw the boy down; and he fell, thrown down, bearing Hari in his heart.
As he fell, the Earth, sustainer of the world, came and held him, devoted to Keshava, the sustainer of the world.
Then, seeing him unhurt, his bones and joints unbroken, Hiranyakashipu said to Shambara, best of wielders of magic:
This ill-behaved boy cannot be killed by us; you know magic, so destroy him by magic.
I shall destroy him, lord of the daityas; see the power of my magic — see here a thousand, and a hundred crores, of magic powers.
Then the asura Shambara, evil-minded, wishing his destruction, let loose his magic powers against Prahlada, who saw all things equally.
With a collected mind and without malice even toward Shambara, Maitreya, Prahlada remembered Madhusudana.
Then, commanded by the Blessed One for his protection, the excellent discus Sudarshana came, garlanded with flames;
by that swift discus, protecting the boy's body, Shambara's thousand magic powers were destroyed one by one.
Then the lord of the daityas said to the drying wind: "Quickly, at my command, let this wicked one be brought to destruction."
Saying "So be it," the swift wind entered him, cold and very harsh, most unbearable, to dry up his body.
Knowing himself thus entered by it, the daitya boy held in his heart the great-souled upholder of the earth.
Then Janardana, dwelling in his heart, enraged, drank up that most parching wind, and the wind came to destruction.
When all the magic powers were exhausted and the wind had perished, the wise boy went back to his guru's house.
Day after day the teacher made the boy learn the science of polity, composed by Ushanas for kings, which gives the fruits of kingship.
When the guru considered him disciplined and to have mastered the science of polity, he told his father he had been instructed:
Your son Prahlada, lord of the daityas, has been made to master the science of polity; he truly knows what Bhargava taught.
